questions.q_en:
Select the option that corrects the following sentence.

All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold away.
options_en: All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold into.
All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold across.
All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold out.
All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold among.
questions.solution_en:
The original sentence uses the phrase "sold away," which is incorrect in standard English for indicating that all tickets are no longer available. The correct phrasal verb is "sold out," meaning all tickets have been purchased and none remain.

· Option A ("sold into") is incorrect as it implies selling something into a specific condition or place, which doesn't fit the context.

· Option B ("sold across") is not a standard phrasal verb in this context and sounds unnatural.

· Option C ("sold out") accurately conveys that all tickets are sold, aligning with common usage (e.g., "The concert is sold out").

· Option D ("sold among") suggests distribution among a group, which is irrelevant here.

Thus, the corrected sentence is: "All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold out."

Directions [Set of 4 Questions]:Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) says these antibiotic-resistant "superbug infections" pose a major "global threat" to public health. Such resistance directly caused 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019, according to The Lancet, a medical journal. The toll is projected to rise to 10 million deaths per year by 2050, says the WHO. Antibiotics - which are considered to be the first line of defence against severe infections - did not work in most of these cases. India has the highest rate of human antibiotic use in the world. Antibiotic-resistant neonatal infections alone are responsible for the deaths of nearly 60,000 newborns each year. Researchers say the use of antibiotics was exacerbated during the Covid-19 pandemic. The weeks-long Kumbh Mela occurs in four Indian cities. The pilgrims take a holy dip in the river waters on the banks of the cities where the festival is held. The US-based researchers gathered data from some 70,000 patients who turned up at more than 40 clinics at two editions of the festival in 2013 and 2015 held in the cities of Prayagraj - also known as Allahabad - and Nashik.

More than 100 million pilgrims attended the two festivals. In Prayagraj in 2013, the patients had a median age of 46 years and most of them were men. Their common symptoms included fever, cough, runny nose, muscle pain, and diarrhoea. Researchers found that more than a third of patients at the clinics were prescribed antibiotics. In Prayagraj, nearly 69% of the patients reporting upper respiratory tract infections received antibiotics at the free state-run clinics at the festival site. "This is an alarmingly high rate, given that the vast majority of upper respiratory tract infections are viral in nature," the researchers say in a recently published paper. Researchers found that entering a clinic at the Kumbh Mela for any reason carried a one-in-three likelihood of walking out with a prescription for antibiotics. If you sought help for a runny nose, the probability increased to two in three. "When antibiotics were prescribed, there appeared to be little rhyme or reason to guide their selection," the researchers said.

Why are antibiotics so important?
options_en: Because they are a part of our immune system.
They are the protectors against infections.
Without them, medicines do not work.
questions.solution_en:
As per the following sentence from the first paragraph, "Antibiotics - which are considered to be the first line of defence against severe infections - did not work on most of these cases", it can be noted that antibiotics protect us from various infections, and which is why they are so important.

Hence, the correct answer is option (b).

(a) encourage individuals to seek timely support,

(b) raising awareness about mental health issues

(c) and foster a more compassionate

(d) helps to reduce stigma,

(e) and understanding society overall
questions.solution_en:
(b) Raising awareness about mental health issues - This gerund phrase serves as the subject of the sentence, introducing the main action being discussed.

(d) helps to reduce stigma, - This is the main verb phrase ("helps") for the subject in (b), followed by the first benefit or outcome ("to reduce stigma"). So far: "Raising awareness about mental health issues helps to reduce stigma,"

(a) encourage individuals to seek timely support, - This infinitive phrase (with "to" implied from "helps to") presents the second benefit, parallel in structure to "reduce stigma." It logically follows (d): "...helps to reduce stigma, encourage individuals to seek timely support,"

(c) and foster a more compassionate - This phrase, beginning with "and," introduces the third benefit, continuing the list of positive outcomes. The verb "foster" is also parallel. Now: "...encourage individuals to seek timely support, and foster a more compassionate"

(e) and understanding society overall - This completes the description of the type of society fostered, with "and understanding" being parallel to "compassionate." It forms the object of "foster."

Final sentence: "Raising awareness about mental health issues helps to reduce stigma, encourage individuals to seek timely support, and foster a more compassionate and understanding society overall."

Hence, option (d) is the answer.

questions.q_en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in reported speech.

He said to the mechanic, "Will you have the car ready by tomorrow morning?"
options_en: He asked the mechanic if he would have the car ready by the next morning.
He told the mechanic if he will have the car ready for the next morning.
He asked the mechanic if he will have the car ready by the previous morning.
He said the mechanic whether he would has the car ready by the following morning.
questions.solution_en:
The original sentence is a question in direct speech. In reported speech, a question beginning with "Will" changes to "if/whether" and the verb shifts to the conditional "would." The phrase "tomorrow morning" becomes "the next morning" to reflect the time shift in reported speech. Option (a) correctly applies these rules: "asked" indicates a question, "if" introduces the reported question, and "would have" is the correct verb form. The other options contain grammatical errors or incorrect time references.

Option b: He told the mechanic if he will have the car ready for the next morning. "Told" is incorrect for a question (questions use "asked"). Additionally, "will" should be "would" in reported speech, and "for the next morning" is less precise than "by the next morning."

Option c: He asked the mechanic if he will have the car ready by the previous morning. "Will" should be "would" in reported speech, and "previous morning" is incorrect, as "tomorrow morning" should become "the next morning" in the context of reported speech.

Option d: He said the mechanic whether he would has the car ready by the following morning. "Said" is incorrect for a question (should be "asked"), "would has" is grammatically incorrect (should be "would have"), and the structure is awkward.

Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

questions.q_en:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

The young boy displayed an aptitude on scientific research.
questions.solution_en:
The most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence is 'aptitude for'. The preposition "on" does not correctly convey the relationship between "aptitude" and "scientific research". The preposition 'on' is used to indicate surface position. "For" is the correct preposition to use with the noun "aptitude" when referring to a natural ability or talent in a particular field or activity. The phrase "aptitude for" indicates that the young boy possesses a talent or ability suited to the field of scientific research. The other prepositions do not convey the intended meaning. "At" typically refers to a specific location or point in time. It does not indicate a proficiency or ability in a particular field or activity. "By" is often used to indicate the agent or means by which something is done. "Aptitude in" is less commonly used compared to "aptitude for" when indicating a natural ability or talent in a specific field or activity. "In" is typically used to describe a state or condition within a certain domain, but "for" is more commonly used to express suitability or proficiency in a particular area. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

The correct sentence is: "The young boy displayed an aptitude for scientific research."

NOTE:

A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence.

Examples

I. The teacher scolded the child for being late.

II. We're going to a party.

· The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.

· The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition.

· The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.

questions.q_en:
Fill in the blank with a suitable article from among the choices given below it.

We enjoyed our visit to ____ Louvre Museum in Paris.
questions.solution_en:
The correct option to fill in the blank is 'the'. The definite article "the" is used before specific nouns that are known to both the speaker and the listener. In this case, "the Louvre Museum in Paris" refers to a specific and well-known cultural institution, making "the" the appropriate choice. Indefinite articles ('a' and 'an') are used when referring to non-specific or generic items. In the given sentence, the speaker is specifically talking about their visit to the Louvre Museum in Paris, which is a unique and well-known museum. Choosing "a" or "an" in this context would imply that there are multiple Louvre Museums, and the speaker happened to visit one of them, but that's not the case. The Louvre Museum in Paris is a singular and distinctive institution. So, the definite article "the" is more appropriate to indicate the specific and well-known nature of the museum. Hence, (b) is the correct answer.

The complete sentence is: We enjoyed our visit to the Louvre Museum in Paris.

NOTE:

Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

questions.q_en:
Directions [Set of 4 Questions]: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

With cracked plaster and peeling paint, I considered what I could say. Water damage would've been the easy answer, but I opted for the truth: "My phone rang." As expected, these words settled somewhere beyond her reach, so she gave my comment its only sensible response: "Maybe you should turn down the ringer." "Come here, let me explain why I hate phones, and why my father is to blame. He was a troubled man," I said, because that's how it had been said to me. She listened with attentive eyes, but I knew she'd be confused by what I said next: "And he'd play Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera. Over and over." She lowered her head in search of a link and looked up when she found one. "Is that solitaire?" This time I allowed a smile. "Sometimes he'd conduct an invisible orchestra, waving arms in an erratic fashion, and sometimes he'd sit and listen. But Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, that one commanded a different reaction. From the start, he stood at full attention, motionless until the end. It went like this for a long time, then he left."

"I soon became his replacement. I'd sit in the study and listen to his music. One evening mother said he wanted to talk to me. I asked if I was going to see him and she said that he'd call. I asked if I could use the phone in his study and she said I could." At this point my companion, attentive as ever, offered her second assumption of the evening, and though more likely than the first, it was just as wrong: "And he never called and that's why you hate phones." No, that's not why. "When mother told me he was on the line, I rushed to the study and dropped the needle on Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, then picked up the phone. He didn't say hello or ask how I was, he only said that there's no peace in the world. He'd looked, it wasn't there, not for him." With her final assumption, she came closer to the truth: "So phones remind you of your father, and that's why you hate them."

"That's part of it," I said, "but there's more. He said he could hear Vivaldi in the background and told me to keep listening, that aria was on to something. Then he said goodbye to me and mother and everyone else. Forever. He found his peace." The music prevented a silence that would've felt more comfortable, then it finally stopped and I let the silence prevail. And there we sat, speaking without speaking, until the silence was shattered by a ring. I stood and walked to the phone, picked it up, not just the receiver, but all of it, and paused to admire the artistry.

What caused the speaker to sabotage his/her phone?
options_en: The speaker didn't like the ringtone.
Because their father didn't call, the speaker ruined the phone.
The speaker had found comfort in silence since their father's departure.
The behaviour of the speaker's father made them hate music.
questions.solution_en: The last paragraph of the passage states that the speaker found console in silence and escaped the memories of her father. So, option (c) is the correct choice.
questions.solution_hi: The last paragraph of the passage states that the speaker found console in silence and escaped the memories of her father. So, option (c) is the correct choice.

questions.q_en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in reported speech.

Chris said to Mary, "Get the dog in the flat before I throw it through this window."
options_en: Chris ordered Mary to get the dog in the flat before he threw it through that window.
Chris ordered Mary to get the dog in the flat before I threw that through this window.
Chris requested Mary to get the dog in the flat before him threw it through that window.
Chris ordered Mary to get the dog in the flat before him to throw it through that window.
questions.solution_en:
Imperative Sentences are used to demonstrate Request, Order, Command, etc.

Imperative Sentences begin with Principal verbs like Go, Make, etc.

As per the meaning of "Said", "Say", etc. the verbs changes forms like "begged/beg" etc.

'To' is used before the Principal Verbs in the Indirect Speech.

For example:

John said to his assistant, "Bring a glass of water." (Direct Speech)

John ordered his assistant to bring him a glass of water. (Indirect Speech)

The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:

· The reporting verb 'said to' is changed into 'ordered'.

· The verb 'get' is changed into the infinitive 'to get'.

· The verb 'throw' (simple present) is changed into 'threw' (simple past).

· The pronoun 'I' is changed into 'he'.

· 'This window' is changed into 'that window'.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Chris ordered Mary to get the dog in the flat before he threw it through that window.

Hence, the answer is option a).

Note:

Infinitive: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, often preceded by to.

Consider the sentences given below:

· To err is human. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to err' is the subject of the verb 'is']

· My father likes to cook. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to cook' is the object of the verb 'likes']

· To vote in elections is our right. [the infinitive 'to vote', like a noun, is the subject of the verb 'is', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (elections)]

· Radha went to the lake to fetch water. [the infinitive 'to fetch', like a noun, is the object of the verb 'went', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (water)]

· The above sentences illustrate various ways in which infinitives are used. It can both act as a noun and a verb.

questions.q_en: Select the option that is NOT an example of direct speech.
options_en: Father, I want to pursue course on handicrafts and not engineering.
I am going to Delhi for an international seminar, Shruti said.
The lady enquired whether there were enough chocolates for the kids.
My father said, why were you late for the dance performance?
questions.solution_en:
In case of Indirect speech, the interrogative sentence contains words or phrases like "enquired (of)", "wanted to know", "asked", etc. Also, the verb is always placed after the subject, unlike in Direct Speech.

For example:

The teacher said to him, "What is your name?" (Direct Speech)

The teacher asked him what his name was. (Indirect Speech)

Among the given options, only (c) matches the conditions. Hence, (c) is the correct answer.
